subject: Chemistry
title: p-Block Elements (Groups 13–18)
summary: p-block elements fill the np subshell (ns²np¹⁻⁶). Across a group, non-metallic character falls and metallic character rises as size increases.
The inert pair effect makes the lower oxidation state more stable for heavy elements: Tl⁺ over Tl³⁺, Pb²⁺ over Pb⁴⁺, Bi³⁺ over Bi⁵⁺.
The first member of each group is anomalous: small size, high electronegativity, no d orbitals (maximum covalency 4) and strong pπ–pπ multiple bonding (N≡N, O=O, C=O).
Exams focus on structures and shapes (VSEPR), acid strength and thermal stability trends of hydrides and oxoacids, and important compounds (NH₃, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, ozone, interhalogens, xenon fluorides).

formulas.name: General configuration
formulas.formula: ns² np¹⁻⁶;  group number = 10 + valence electrons

formulas.name: Inert pair effect
formulas.formula: stability of the lower state (group oxidation state − 2) increases down the group
formulas.when: Tl⁺ > Tl³⁺, Pb²⁺ > Pb⁴⁺, Bi³⁺ > Bi⁵⁺.
formulas.note: PbO₂ and Bi(V) compounds are therefore strong oxidising agents.

formulas.name: Hydrides of group 15
formulas.formula: NH₃ > PH₃ > AsH₃ > SbH₃ > BiH₃: basicity and thermal stability decrease; reducing character increases;  bond angle NH₃ 107° > PH₃ 93.6°
formulas.mistake: Boiling point: PH₃ < AsH₃ < NH₃ < SbH₃ < BiH₃ — NH₃ is anomalously high (hydrogen bonding), not the lowest.

formulas.name: Hydrides of group 16
formulas.formula: H₂O < H₂S < H₂Se < H₂Te: acidity increases;  thermal stability decreases down the group
formulas.note: Water has an anomalously high boiling point because of hydrogen bonding.

formulas.name: Hydrogen halides
formulas.formula: acid strength: HF < HCl < HBr < HI;  bond strength and thermal stability: HF > HCl > HBr > HI
formulas.note: HF is the WEAKEST acid in water despite F being most electronegative — the H–F bond is very strong.

formulas.name: Oxoacids of chlorine
formulas.formula: acid strength: HOCl < HClO₂ < HClO₃ < HClO₄;  oxidising power: the reverse

formulas.name: Phosphorus oxoacids (basicity = P–OH bonds)
formulas.formula: H₃PO₂ monobasic (2 P–H, reducing);  H₃PO₃ dibasic (1 P–H, reducing);  H₃PO₄ tribasic (no P–H)
formulas.mistake: Count only O–H bonds attached to P for basicity — P–H hydrogens are not acidic.

formulas.name: Shapes of interhalogens
formulas.formula: XX′ linear;  XX′₃ (ClF₃) T-shaped;  XX′₅ (BrF₅) square pyramidal;  XX′₇ (IF₇) pentagonal bipyramidal

formulas.name: Xenon fluorides
formulas.formula: XeF₂ linear (sp³d);  XeF₄ square planar (sp³d²);  XeF₆ distorted octahedral (sp³d³);  XeO₃ pyramidal

formulas.name: Key preparations
formulas.formula: NH₃: Haber process (Fe catalyst, ~200 atm, ~700 K);  HNO₃: Ostwald process (Pt/Rh, NH₃ oxidation);  H₂SO₄: contact process (V₂O₅ catalyst, SO₂ → SO₃)

formulas.name: Structures of sulphur and phosphorus
formulas.formula: white P: P₄ tetrahedral, reactive, glows;  red P: polymeric, less reactive;  rhombic S (S₈ crowns) stable below 369 K;  monoclinic above

formulas.name: Group 13 & 14 highlights
formulas.formula: boric acid H₃BO₃ is a weak monobasic Lewis acid (accepts OH⁻);  diborane B₂H₆ has two 3-centre-2-electron (banana) bonds;  CO is a neutral oxide and good ligand; CO₂ acidic; SiO₂ covalent network
formulas.when: Questions on B, Al, C, Si compounds.

examples.title: Why is HF weak?
examples.problem: Explain why HF is a weaker acid than HCl in water.
examples.solution: The H–F bond is very strong and F⁻ is small and strongly hydrated, so HF ionises only slightly; acid strength rises down the group as the H–X bond weakens.

examples.title: Basicity of H₃PO₃
examples.problem: How many replaceable hydrogens does H₃PO₃ have?
examples.solution: Structure HP(O)(OH)₂: two P–OH bonds → dibasic; the P–H hydrogen is not acidic but makes H₃PO₃ a reducing agent.

examples.title: Shape of XeF₄
examples.solution: Xe has 8 valence electrons: 4 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 6 pairs (octahedral arrangement, sp³d²). The lone pairs sit opposite each other, so the molecule is square planar.

examples.title: Shape of ClF₃
examples.solution: Cl: 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 5 pairs (trigonal bipyramidal). Lone pairs take equatorial positions, leaving a T-shaped molecule.

examples.title: Brown ring test
examples.problem: What forms the brown ring in the test for nitrate?
examples.solution: Fe²⁺ reduces NO₃⁻ to NO in conc. H₂SO₄; NO binds to iron forming [Fe(H₂O)₅NO]²⁺, seen as a brown ring at the interface.

examples.title: Inert pair effect
examples.problem: Why is PbO₂ a strong oxidising agent?
examples.solution: Down group 14, the 6s² pair resists bonding (inert pair effect), so Pb²⁺ is more stable than Pb⁴⁺. PbO₂ (Pb⁴⁺) readily gains electrons to become Pb²⁺.

topics.title: Group 13 (B, Al, Ga, In, Tl)
topics.explain: B is a non-metal and forms covalent compounds; Al is amphoteric. Boron halides are Lewis acids (BF₃ < BCl₃ < BBr₃ in acid strength due to back-bonding). AlCl₃ exists as a dimer Al₂Cl₆. Borax and boric acid are important boron compounds.

topics.title: Group 14 (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb)
topics.explain: Carbon shows catenation (strongest C–C bonds) and allotropes: diamond (sp³, hardest), graphite (sp², conducts electricity, lubricant), fullerenes (C₆₀). Silicones and silicates contain Si–O chains; zeolites are aluminosilicates used as catalysts.

topics.title: Group 15 (N, P, As, Sb, Bi)
topics.explain: N₂ is inert because of the strong triple bond (941 kJ/mol). Nitrogen oxides: N₂O, NO (paramagnetic, odd electron), N₂O₃, NO₂ (paramagnetic, dimerises to N₂O₄), N₂O₅. PCl₅ is trigonal bipyramidal in gas and [PCl₄]⁺[PCl₆]⁻ in the solid. Common oxidation states −3, +3, +5; all members form hydrides EH₃ (NH₃, PH₃, AsH₃ arsine, SbH₃, BiH₃) and oxides E₂O₃ and E₂O₅ — Sb₂O₅ does exist; only the +5 state of Bi is unstable (inert pair effect). NH₃/NH₄⁺ test: Nessler's reagent (K₂HgI₄ in KOH) gives a brown precipitate (basic mercury(II) amido-iodide).

topics.title: Group 16 (O, S, Se, Te, Po)
topics.explain: O₂ is paramagnetic. Ozone (O₃) is bent, a strong oxidising agent, and protects us from UV. Oxides can be acidic (SO₂), basic (CaO), amphoteric (Al₂O₃) or neutral (CO). H₂SO₄ is a dehydrating agent (chars sugar) and an oxidising agent when hot and concentrated.

topics.title: Group 17 (F, Cl, Br, I)
topics.explain: Halogens are coloured, strong oxidising agents (F₂ strongest) with the most negative electron gain enthalpies (Cl most negative). F shows only −1. Cl₂ bleaches by oxidation (moist), and reacts with cold dilute NaOH to give NaCl + NaOCl and with hot concentrated NaOH to give NaCl + NaClO₃ (disproportionation).

topics.title: Group 18 (noble gases)
topics.explain: Full ns²np⁶ shells, very high ionisation enthalpies. Xenon forms compounds with F and O because its IE is close to that of O₂ (Bartlett made O₂⁺PtF₆⁻, then Xe⁺PtF₆⁻). Uses: He in balloons and diving gas, Ne in signs, Ar as an inert atmosphere in welding and bulbs.

topics.title: Anomalous behaviour summary
topics.explain: The first members (B, C, N, O, F) are small, very electronegative, lack d orbitals (covalency ≤ 4) and form strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds. Heavier members use d orbitals to expand the octet (PCl₅, SF₆) and form dπ–pπ bonds.

ratta: Inert pair: Tl⁺, Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺ more stable.
HF weakest HX acid;  HI strongest.
H₃PO₂ mono, H₃PO₃ di, H₃PO₄ tribasic.
HClO₄ strongest oxoacid of Cl;  HOCl best oxidiser.
XeF₂ linear, XeF₄ square planar, XeF₆ distorted octahedral.
ClF₃ T-shaped;  BrF₅ square pyramidal;  IF₇ pentagonal bipyramidal.
Group 15: −3, +3, +5;  E₂O₃ and E₂O₅ for all (Sb₂O₅ exists; Bi(V) unstable).
Nessler's reagent (K₂HgI₄ + KOH) + NH₃/NH₄⁺ → brown ppt.
1st IE (kJ/mol): B 801 < C 1086 < O 1314 < N 1402 (N > O anomaly).
